subject: geography

moments.title: Almost no one lived in cities
moments.body: In 1800, around 3% of humans lived in settlements over 5,000 people. London was the largest city at about 1 million. The industrial city was about to be invented.
moments.takeaway: Cities of any size are a recent norm. For most of human history, urban life was a tiny exception.

moments.title: London becomes the first 6-million city
moments.body: By 1900, around 14% of the world is urban. London, New York, Paris and Tokyo lead, all between 4-6 million. Industrial concentration, railways, and rural exodus drive the change. Public health crises (cholera in 1850s London, the Great Stink of 1858) had forced sewer systems, water treatment and building codes.
moments.takeaway: Modern urban infrastructure was built in response to industrial-era disease. Bazalgette's London sewers are still in use.

moments.title: Urban majority
moments.body: Around 2007, more than half the world's population lives in cities for the first time. The fastest growth is in Asia and Africa: Lagos, Dhaka, Kinshasa, Delhi. Tokyo (37 million) is the largest metropolitan area.
moments.takeaway: The 21st century is the urban century. Climate adaptation, energy use, political organisation all increasingly flow through cities.

now.title: The megacity problem
now.body: By 2050, roughly 68% of humans are projected to be urban. African and Asian megacities will dominate growth. The 'C40' network of cities now coordinates climate policy independently of national governments. Urban heat islands, informal settlements, water security, transport — geography in the 21st century is largely urban geography.
now.open_questions: Can cities decarbonise fast enough? Can governance scale? Saskia Sassen's 'Global City' framework argues that the largest cities increasingly form their own networked system, partly separated from national context.

reflection: Two centuries of urbanisation has remade not just cities but the species. The 'rural' is now the minority experience for the first time in human history.
